$comment: Declaration-name, call, type-position, and contextual-keyword rules. Every rule here is anchored by a lookbehind on an already-consumed reserved word or by the start of a line, so contextual keywords stay ordinary identifiers everywhere else. Reserved words themselves are never scoped here: they carry the scope the tokenizer-derived keyword rules give them.

contextual-keywords.$comment: The annotation-declaration entry is a begin/end block, not a single-line match: an annotation's parameter list opens multiline mode (GRAMMAR.md 2.1), so the closing ')' and 'targets' keyword may be several physical lines below 'annotation NAME'. The block ends by consuming the real 'targets' separator, which is always immediately preceded (ignoring a run of spaces/tabs) by the closing ')' of a parameter list or by the declaration's own name -- never by punctuation such as '(' or '=' -- so the leading lookbehind and the '(?!\s*:)' guard together keep a same-named parameter or default value (e.g. 'targets: int' or '= targets') from ending the block early. The alternate end branch is a zero-width lookahead bailout that closes the block (without consuming the triggering keyword, so it still gets its normal scope) if another root declaration keyword starts a line first, so a 'targets'-less declaration (mid-edit or malformed) cannot swallow the rest of the file.

dictionary-key.$comment: Scans a dictionary entry forward from its own boundary instead of backward from its separator, so a key of any shape hides the type-shaped token that follows the ':' from the generic #type-positions rule. Per GRAMMAR.md a Python-style entry's key is an arbitrary expression, which no bounded lookbehind can describe; the region therefore opens at an entry boundary (the start of a line inside the dictionary, or right after '{' or ',') and closes on the first ':' that is not nested inside a group. Nesting is handled structurally rather than by counting: #dictionary-parentheses, #dictionary-brackets, and #dictionary-literal consume balanced '(...)', '[...]', and '{...}' regions before the 'end' pattern can see anything inside them, so a ',' or ':' belonging to a call argument list, a subscript, or a lambda signature cannot terminate the key early. The 'end' pattern also bails out at an unconsumed ',' or '}' so a Lua-style 'key = value' entry -- whose separator this rule deliberately does not match, because a plain reassignment inside a nested lambda body is indistinguishable from one -- closes at its own entry boundary rather than swallowing the rest of the dictionary. The trailing type-shaped token is only consumed when it is not itself the callable of a constructor/conversion call (e.g. 'Vector2()'), which #calls must keep scoping normally; the whitespace after ':' is consumed unconditionally so #type-positions cannot start a match there. #contextual-keywords is left out so an accessor-shaped key such as 'get' stays an ordinary identifier.
dictionary-key.name: meta.dictionary.entry.foundryscript

dictionary-parentheses.$comment: Consumes a balanced parenthesized region inside a dictionary -- a lambda's parameter list, a call's argument list, or a grouping in a key -- as a single unit. On the value side this shields the region from #dictionary-key: without it, a parameter declaration that starts its own physical line inside a multiline parameter list -- 'value: int,' on its own line -- would satisfy the entry-boundary anchor and be mistaken for a fresh dictionary entry, suppressing the parameter's real type scope. On the key side it is what keeps a ',' or ':' nested in the key from ending the key region early. The 'end' pattern bails out on an unclosed '(' the moment a '}' appears, without consuming it, so malformed or mid-edit input cannot leave this region open past the dictionary that contains it.
dictionary-parentheses.name: meta.dictionary.parenthesized.foundryscript

dictionary-brackets.$comment: The square-bracket counterpart of #dictionary-parentheses: consumes a balanced '[...]' region -- an array literal on the value side, a subscript on the key side -- as a single unit, so punctuation nested inside it neither opens a spurious entry nor ends a key region early. The same '}' bailout keeps an unclosed '[' from leaking past the dictionary that contains it.
dictionary-brackets.name: meta.dictionary.bracketed.foundryscript
